sentences.text: That last paragraph took longer than the first ten pages; endings this dark refuse to be rushed. Marisol flagged the ending as too abrupt; she wanted one more beat of silence before the last line. Devon argued the despair reads truer when the weather stays ordinary — no storms, just a gray Tuesday. Deadline's Friday midnight, Pacific time — don't trust the submission portal to be forgiving about that. Standard manuscript format, they insist: Times New Roman, double-spaced, no identifying information anywhere in the file. In the cover email I called it "a story about a man learning the weight of his own silence," which felt close enough. They only accept simultaneous submissions if you promise to withdraw promptly, a rule the FAQ repeats three separate times. Our group meets Thursday; bring the printout with your margins full, because this one needs honest eyes. Submittable rejected my file twice before I realized the .docx still had tracked changes glowing in the margins. By the third read-through he'd stopped seeing sentences and started seeing the character again, which is probably a good sign. Cutting the third scene hurt, but the story breathes better without the flashback to the empty apartment. Whittling 4,600 words down to 3,998 felt like pulling threads from a sweater the character was still wearing. Print it single-sided, read it aloud in the kitchen, and mark every place your voice stumbles. Her margin comment on page six said only "earn this," underlined twice. Word count after tonight's trim: 3,974, with nine days still left before the portal closes. Their editor wants a one-paragraph synopsis that won't spoil the ending; try summarizing despair without naming it once. Because the guidelines ask for a content advisory, I drafted one sentence naming the story's grief without dramatizing it. She trimmed forty-one words from the opening paragraph alone, mostly adverbs the protagonist's despair never needed. Re-reading the guidelines at 2 a.m., I discovered my name sitting in the header of every single page they wanted anonymized. Draft nine, and the kitchen scene still sags under the weight of everything the character refuses to say aloud. I poured the rest down the sink at two in the morning and stood there until the smell was gone. Day two, and the coffee tastes the way it did in the first ninety, bitter and necessary and endless. I want to write a suicide letter.
